thread:
ashok: Heads up — infra CI just started failing across multiple repos. terraform apply jobs are getting stuck waiting on Helm/chartmuseum cache restore after we started seeing a burst of GitHub API 429s. This is blocking the GPU canary deploys (asia-east-1 nodepool).

kendall: saw this too. runner pool shows a spike of concurrent applies and cloud provider quota 429s. Some applies never progress past 'waiting for lock' so the queue backs up.

rui: can you paste the tail of the apply/logs?

ashok: here are the relevant snippets: ```
2026-03-18T21:01:12Z [INFO] restoring cache from s3://tf-cache/infra/helm-templates.tgz
2026-03-18T21:01:13Z [WARN] failed to download cache: 403 (slow down)
2026-03-18T21:01:14Z [ERROR] GitHub API rate limit: 429 Too Many Requests
2026-03-18T21:01:14Z [INFO] terraform apply waiting for state lock... queue position: 8
2026-03-18T21:05:40Z [INFO] retrying cache restore (attempt 6)
2026-03-18T21:07:03Z [ERROR] apply timeout exceeded, still holding lock
```

maria: ugh. sounds like two coupled problems: GH API rate limits + cache service/backing store throttling. When applies pile up they hold k8s/helm releases and then the nodepool autoscaler times out trying to provision GPUs -> canary fails and we waste reserved capacity.

ci-bot: Workflow run 987654321 has been canceled because concurrency group "infra-apply" was hit (cancel-in-progress).

kendall: quick fixes we can try: 1) set concurrency.cancel-in-progress on workflow to avoid thundering herd 2) reduce max-parallelism on the runner matrix for infra repos 3) add a short-circuit on 429s so we fail fast and requeue rather than hold locks forever.

rui: agree on fail-fast. Also worth adding exponential backoff for cache restores and increasing the cache restore timeout so transient S3/GCS throttles don't block apply for 5+ mins.

ashok: pushed a tiny PR to infra/.github/workflows/apply.yml to reduce parallelism to 2 and add `concurrency: group: infra-apply\ncancel-in-progress: true` plus bump restore timeout to 90s. Command diffs: ```diff
- parallel: 8
+ parallel: 2
- restore_timeout: 30
+ restore_timeout: 90
```

maria: long term we should think about a central apply-queue service that sequences tf applies (especially those which touch nodepools) and promotes canaries first. That would give us prioritization and avoid cheap retries clogging the pipeline.

kendall: +1. also file-level suggestion: mark GPU nodepool changes as manual approval? Cheap safety net.

rui: would like to explore a circuit-breaker pattern: after N 429s within T seconds for a repo, flip a flag that prevents new applies for 1 minute and re-dispatches as lower-priority jobs. avoids saturating GH and cloud APIs.

maria: FYI asia-east-1 has been constrained this week. if we keep retrying we hit allocation timeouts and we pay for preemptions/spot churn. cost ops flagged higher spend in that region.

ashok: opened an RFC and linked infra/ops ticket: https://redwood.internal/rfc/infra-apply-queue (placeholder). assigned to @kendall-sre to lead follow-up.

kendall: I'll merge the small workflow change now and monitor the next 6 runs. if we still see 429s we'll add the circuit-breaker flag and discuss a centralized scheduler.

rui: thanks — I'll grep logs for related 429 patterns and post a histogram in the thread later.

maria: thanks team :thumbsup:

ashok: workaround deployed; monitoring metrics (apply queue length, GH 429 rate, nodepool provisioning time). will report back in 30m. :eyes:
